'''Multidimensional interpolation''' is the process of finding a multivariable function $f(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ that for a definite set of datapoints $\{(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i},y_i)\mid i\in [0,n], i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ satisfies $f(x_{1,i},\cdots,x_{m,i})=y_i$.

== Grid interpolation ==

=== via Lagrange polynomial in multiple variables ===

If a "grid" of $n^m$ datapoints, i.e., values of $y$ at all possible combinations of $n$ particular values in each of the $m$ variables

$$
\{(x_{1,i_1},\cdots,x_{m,i_m},y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m})\mid i_1,\cdots,i_m \in [0,n-1],\, i_1,\cdots,i_m \in \mathbb{N}\}
$$

is known, then a multivariable-version of the Lagrange polynomial can be used to interpolate for $y$.

$$
P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)=\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}\cdots\sum_{i_m=0}^{n-1}y_{i_1,\cdots,i_m}\prod_{j=1}^{m}L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j),\qquad L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j)=\prod_{\substack{k=0\\k\neq i_j}}^{n-1}\frac{x_j-x_{j,k}}{x_{j,i_j}-x_{j,k}}
$$

which is a multi-variable polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ in each variable unique for each set of datapoints.

Similar to the [[Polynomial_interpolation#Lagrange_polynomial|one-dimensional Lagrange polynomial]]s,

$$
L^{(x_j)}_{i_j}(x_j)=
\begin{cases}
1, & x_j=x_{j,i_j},\\
0, & x_j=x_{j,i_k},\, i_k \in  [0,n-1],\, i_k \neq i_j,\, i_k \in \mathbb{N}
\end{cases}
$$

which guarantees that $P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)=y(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ at all datapoints.<ref>{{#cite:Q2392}}</ref>

<blockquote>
$P(x_1,\cdots,x_m)$ is also known as the '''tensor product Lagrange interpolant'''.
</blockquote>

{{Hidden example}}
'''Surface temperature over a square of weather stations.''' 

Sixteen weather stations sitting in a $4^\circ \times 4^\circ$ grid measure surface temperature at various latitudes and longitudes.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Temperature ($^\circ$C) at each station
! latitude $\downarrow$ / longitude $\rightarrow$ !! $0^\circ$E !! $1^\circ$E !! $2^\circ$E !! $3^\circ$E
|-
! $53^\circ$N
| 18.4 || 19.1 || 20.6 || 21.8
|-
! $52^\circ$N
| 20.1 || 20.9 || 22.3 || 23.5
|-
! $51^\circ$N
| 21.7 || 22.5 || 23.9 || 25.0
|-
! $50^\circ$N
| 22.8 || 23.6 || 24.9 || 26.1
|}

What is the interpolated temperature at $51.6^\circ \textbf{N}, 1.4^\circ \textbf{E}$?

'''Algebraic solution''':

Let $x_1$ represent the latitude, $x_2$ represent the longitude, and denote the surface temperature reading at row $i_1$, column $i_2$ by $y_{i_1,i_2}$.

Then the interpolating multi-variable Lagrange polynomial is 
$$
P(x_1,x_2)=\sum_{i_1=1}^{4}\sum_{i_2=1}^{4}y_{i_1,i_2}\,L^{(x_1)}_{i_1}(x_1)\,L^{(x_2)}_{i_2}(x_2)
$$

where

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)=-\frac{(x_1-51)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{6}=-\frac{1}{6}x_1^3+26x_1^2-\frac{8111}{6}x_1+23426,\\ 
L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-52)(x_1-53)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}x_1^3-\frac{155}{2}x_1^2+4003x_1-68900
$$

$$
L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)=-\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-53)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}x_1^3+77x_1^2-\frac{7903}{2}x_1+67575,\\
L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)=\frac{(x_1-50)(x_1-51)(x_1-52)}{6}=\frac{1}{6}x_1^3-\frac{51}{2}x_1^2+\frac{3901}{3}x_1-22100
$$

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)=-\frac{(x_2-1)(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{6}=-\frac{1}{6}x_2^3+x_2^2-\frac{11}{6}x_2+1,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-2)(x_2-3)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}x_2^3-\frac{5}{2}x_2^2+3x_2
$$

$$
L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)=-\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-3)}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}x_2^3+2x_2^2-\frac{3}{2}x_2,\qquad L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)=\frac{x_2(x_2-1)(x_2-2)}{6}=\frac{1}{6}x_2^3-\frac{1}{2}x_2^2+\frac{1}{3}x_2
$$

Hence 

$$
P(x_1,x_2)=22.8\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+23.6\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+24.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+26.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{1}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+21.7\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+22.5\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+23.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+25.0\,L^{(x_1)}_{2}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+20.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+20.9\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+22.3\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+23.5\,L^{(x_1)}_{3}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

$$
{}+18.4\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{1}(x_2)+19.1\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{2}(x_2)+20.6\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{3}(x_2)+21.8\,L^{(x_1)}_{4}(x_1)L^{(x_2)}_{4}(x_2)
$$

On simplification:

$$
P(x_1,x_2)=-\tfrac{1}{45}x_1^3x_2^3+\tfrac{11}{120}x_1^3x_2^2-\tfrac{31}{360}x_1^3x_2+\tfrac{1}{15}x_1^3+\tfrac{103}{30}x_1^2x_2^3-\tfrac{283}{20}x_1^2x_2^2+\tfrac{199}{15}x_1^2x_2-\tfrac{209}{20}x_1^2
$$

$$
{}-\tfrac{31823}{180}x_1x_2^3+\tfrac{87361}{120}x_1x_2^2-\tfrac{245249}{360}x_1x_2+\tfrac{32657}{60}x_1+\tfrac{45511}{15}x_2^3-\tfrac{62416}{5}x_2^2+\tfrac{174899}{15}x_2-\tfrac{93997}{10}
$$

Substitute in $x_1=51.6,x_2=1.4$,

$$
P(51.6,1.4)=-\tfrac{1}{45}(51.6)^3(1.4)^3+\tfrac{11}{120}(51.6)^3(1.4)^2-\tfrac{31}{360}(51.6)^3(1.4)+\tfrac{1}{15}(51.6)^3
$$

$$
{}+\tfrac{103}{30}(51.6)^2(1.4)^3-\tfrac{283}{20}(51.6)^2(1.4)^2+\tfrac{199}{15}(51.6)^2(1.4)-\tfrac{209}{20}(51.6)^2
$$

$$
{}-\tfrac{31823}{180}(51.6)(1.4)^3+\tfrac{87361}{120}(51.6)(1.4)^2-\tfrac{245249}{360}(51.6)(1.4)+\tfrac{32657}{60}(51.6)
$$

$$
{}+\tfrac{45511}{15}(1.4)^3-\tfrac{62416}{5}(1.4)^2+\tfrac{174899}{15}(1.4)-\tfrac{93997}{10}=22.1162
$$

'''Numerical solution''':

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import sympy as sp

x1, x2 = sp.symbols('x1 x2')

def lagrange_basis(nodes, x):
    """The Lagrange basis polynomials on `nodes`, from the product formula."""
    basis = []
    for i in nodes:
        p = sp.Integer(1)
        for k in nodes:
            if k != i:
                p *= (x - k) / (i - k)
        basis.append(sp.expand(p))
    return basis

latitude = [50, 51, 52, 53]                 # nodes of x1
longitude = [0, 1, 2, 3]                    # nodes of x2
L1 = lagrange_basis(latitude, x1)           # L^(x1)_1 .. L^(x1)_4
L2 = lagrange_basis(longitude, x2)          # L^(x2)_1 .. L^(x2)_4
print(L1)
print(L2)

temperature = [[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
               [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
               [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
               [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]]    # row = latitude 50, 51, 52, 53; column = longitude 0, 1, 2, 3

# one term per station: reading times its x1 polynomial times its x2 polynomial
p = sp.expand(sum(sp.Rational(str(temperature[j][i])) * L1[j] * L2[i]
                  for j in range(4) for i in range(4)))
print(p)

value = p.subs({x1: sp.Rational('51.6'), x2: sp.Rational('1.4')})   # 51.6 N, 1.4 E
print(value)
print(float(value))
</syntaxhighlight>

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

latitude = np.array([50.0, 51.0, 52.0, 53.0])        # nodes of x1
longitude = np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0])           # nodes of x2
temperature = np.array([[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
                        [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
                        [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
                        [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]])   # row = latitude, column = longitude

def L(nodes, x):
    """The Lagrange basis polynomials on `nodes`, evaluated at x."""
    return np.array([np.prod([(x - k) / (i - k) for k in nodes if k != i]) for i in nodes])

def p(x1, x2):
    """2-variable Lagrange polynomial"""
    return (temperature * np.outer(basis_at(latitude, x1), L(longitude, x2))).sum()

lon_plot = np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 121)
lat_plot = np.linspace(50.0, 53.0, 121)
surface = np.array([[p(x, y) for y in lon_plot] for x in lat_plot])

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.0, 6.8))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
ax.set_box_aspect((1.35, 1.0, 0.62))
mesh_lon, mesh_lat = np.meshgrid(lon_plot, lat_plot)
surf = ax.plot_surface(mesh_lon, mesh_lat, surface, cmap="RdYlBu_r", linewidth=0,
                       antialiased=True, rstride=2, cstride=2, alpha=0.92)
ax.scatter(np.tile(longitude, 4), np.repeat(latitude, 4), temperature.ravel(),
           s=70, color="#c0392b", edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.9,
           depthshade=False, label="16 weather stations")
ax.scatter([1.4], [51.6], [f(51.6, 1.4)], s=170, color="black", marker="X",
           depthshade=False, label=r"query point (1.4$^\circ$E, 51.6$^\circ$N)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"longitude ($^\circ$E)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_ylabel(r"latitude ($^\circ$N)", labelpad=10)
ax.set_zlabel(r"temperature ($^\circ$C)", labelpad=8)
ax.set_xticks(longitude)
ax.set_yticks(latitude)
ax.set_zlim(16.5, 26.5)
ax.view_init(elev=34, azim=-56)
fig.colorbar(surf, shrink=0.55, pad=0.10, aspect=24,
             label=r"interpolated temperature ($^\circ$C)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

== Pointwise interpolation ==

Pointwise interpolation (or '''point evaluation''') asks only for the value of $f$ at one new point $(x_1^*,\cdots,x_m^*)$ inside the data range, without constructing $f$ anywhere else. It fixes what is to be computed, not how $f$ is defined: the rule of interpolation is free, and only one number is wanted out of it.

'''One variable at a time.''' A grid is a family of lines, one along each variable, and each of those lines is an ordinary one-dimensional dataset. A one-dimensional rule applied to the lines of one direction, and then to the lines of the next, reaches the query point. [[Person:Jeffrey R. Chasnov|Chasnov]] states the two-variable case in full: on an $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ grid, first perform $n+1$ one-dimensional interpolations to find the interpolant at the $n+1$ points $(x_0,y^*),\cdots,(x_n,y^*)$, then a single one-dimensional interpolation to find it at $(x^*,y^*)$; MATLAB's <code>interp2</code> and <code>interp3</code> address exactly this problem<ref>{{#cite:Q2421}}</ref>.

'''The rule, named once.''' Let

$$
\mathcal{I}\big[\{v_k\}_{k=0}^{n-1}\big](t)
$$

be the value at $t$ that the chosen rule gives to readings $v_0,\cdots,v_{n-1}$ at nodes $t_0,\cdots,t_{n-1}$. The rule may be [[Piecewise_linear_interpolation|piecewise linear]], a cubic spline with whatever end condition ([[Cubic_spline_interpolation|cubic spline interpolation]]), a monotone scheme, or a single polynomial through the whole line; only the arithmetic inside a pass changes.

'''Two variables.''' With readings $y_{i_1,i_2}$ on $n$ nodes per axis, a pass along $x_2$ holds $x_1$ at each of its nodes in turn:

$$
y^*_{i_1}=\mathcal{I}\big[\{y_{i_1,i_2}\}_{i_2=0}^{n-1}\big](x_2^*),\qquad \forall i_1\in [0,n-1],\, i_1 \in \mathbb{N}
$$

The $n$ values $y^*_{i_1}$ are the interpolant at $(x_{1,i_1},x_2^*)$, i.e., readings on the line $x_2=x_2^*$, so one more pass finishes:

$$
f(x_1^*,x_2^*)\approx\mathcal{I}\big[\{y^*_{i_1}\}_{i_1=0}^{n-1}\big](x_1^*)
$$

'''$m$ variables.''' Each pass removes one variable, leaving $n^{m-1}$ values, then $n^{m-2}$, down to one, so the passes cost $n^{m-1},n^{m-2},\cdots,n^0$ interpolations whatever the rule, that is $(n^m-1)/(n-1)$ in all; for $n=4$ and $m=2,3,4$ that is $5$, $21$, and $85$. A rule that reads only the nodes bracketing its target needs only the lines that bracket the target, so a local rule costs two readings a line and two lines a pass.

'''Any order.''' For a rule linear in its readings, with weights $\varphi_k$ fixed by the nodes and by the target, the two passes give

$$
f(x_1^*,x_2^*)=\sum_{i_1=0}^{n-1}\sum_{i_2=0}^{n-1}\varphi^{(1)}_{i_1}(x_1^*)\,\varphi^{(2)}_{i_2}(x_2^*)\,y_{i_1,i_2}
$$

whose products are the same under either nesting, so the order of the passes is free<ref>{{#cite:Q2391}}</ref>.

'''The station grid again, by hand.''' Take the sixteen readings of [[#Grid_interpolation|grid interpolation]] and the query at $1.4^\circ$E, $51.6^\circ$N, and take the rule for a line of unit spacing to be the cubic through its four readings, written in differences:

$$
C(u)=w_0+\Delta w_0\,u+\frac{\Delta^2 w_0}{2}u(u-1)+\frac{\Delta^3 w_0}{6}u(u-1)(u-2)
$$

where $u$ is the distance from the first node and $\Delta$ is the forward difference of the line's readings. On four nodes this is what a not-a-knot spline gives as well, a single cubic piece spanning the line. At $u=1.4$ the last two coefficients are $u(u-1)/2=0.28$ and $u(u-1)(u-2)/6=-0.056$, the same on every parallel, so each longitude pass costs three multiplications on top of its reading:

* $50^\circ$N, $\Delta=(0.8,1.3,1.2)$, $\Delta^2=(0.5,-0.1)$, $\Delta^3=-0.6$: $22.8+1.4(0.8)+0.28(0.5)-0.056(-0.6)=24.0936$
* $51^\circ$N, $\Delta=(0.8,1.4,1.1)$, $\Delta^2=(0.6,-0.3)$, $\Delta^3=-0.9$: $21.7+1.4(0.8)+0.28(0.6)-0.056(-0.9)=23.0384$
* $52^\circ$N, $\Delta=(0.8,1.4,1.2)$, $\Delta^2=(0.6,-0.2)$, $\Delta^3=-0.8$: $20.1+1.4(0.8)+0.28(0.6)-0.056(-0.8)=21.4328$
* $53^\circ$N, $\Delta=(0.7,1.5,1.2)$, $\Delta^2=(0.8,-0.3)$, $\Delta^3=-1.1$: $18.4+1.4(0.7)+0.28(0.8)-0.056(-1.1)=19.6656$

Those four are readings on the line $x_1=1.4$, and the same rule on them at $u=1.6$, where $u(u-1)/2=0.48$ and $u(u-1)(u-2)/6=-0.064$, gives

$$
24.0936+1.6(-1.0552)+0.48(-0.5504)-0.064(0.3888)=22.1162048
$$

the number [[#Grid_interpolation|grid interpolation]] reached by summing its 16 monomials, obtained here without forming any of them.

The same passes in code, with the rule passed in as an argument:

<syntaxhighlight lang="python" copy>
import numpy as np
from scipy.interpolate import CubicSpline

temperature = np.array([[22.8, 23.6, 24.9, 26.1],
                        [21.7, 22.5, 23.9, 25.0],
                        [20.1, 20.9, 22.3, 23.5],
                        [18.4, 19.1, 20.6, 21.8]])   # row = latitude, column = longitude

def passes(nodes, values, point, rule):
    """Value at `point` of the grid interpolant, one one-dimensional pass per variable.

    nodes  -- node coordinates of each variable, in the order of the axes of `values`
    values -- m-dimensional array of readings, values[i_1, ..., i_m]
    rule   -- rule(nodes, readings, t), the one-dimensional rule evaluated at t
    """
    data = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    for axis, target in enumerate(point):         # one pass per variable, first axis first
        data = np.apply_along_axis(
            lambda line: rule(np.asarray(nodes[axis], dtype=float), line, target), 0, data)
    return float(data)

linear  = lambda nodes, line, t: float(np.interp(t, nodes, line))
spline  = lambda nodes, line, t: float(CubicSpline(nodes, line)(t))
natural = lambda nodes, line, t: float(CubicSpline(nodes, line, bc_type="natural")(t))

latitude, longitude = np.arange(50.0, 54.0), np.arange(0.0, 4.0)
for name, rule in [("piecewise linear", linear), ("natural cubic spline", natural),
                   ("not-a-knot cubic spline", spline)]:
    print(name, passes([latitude, longitude], temperature, [51.6, 1.4], rule))
</syntaxhighlight>

The spline line prints the value worked out above; the natural end condition gives $22.1157$ instead, and swapping the two variables in <code>nodes</code> and in <code>point</code> alike, with the readings transposed, returns the same three values.

<blockquote>
A rule that reads only the nodes bracketing its target does far less of this arithmetic. Piecewise linear passes at the same point touch only the four stations surrounding it: $0.6(22.5)+0.4(23.9)=23.06$ and $0.6(20.9)+0.4(22.3)=21.46$ along the parallels, then $0.4(23.06)+0.6(21.46)=22.10$ along the meridian. That is $0.02\ ^\circ$C from the grid interpolant, but the two are not interchangeable: the bilinear interpolant is merely continuous where cells meet, whereas the grid interpolant is a single polynomial and therefore smooth everywhere.
</blockquote>
